source_version: Capella (continuously deployed, no discrete version number)

relations.subject: sso:realm
relations.evidence:
Choose to turn on or off group mapping.  
Group mapping allows you to assign roles to SSO users based on which teams map to their SSO group.

relations.subject: sso:realm
relations.evidence:
Choose a default team.  
Capella automatically assigns users to the chosen default team when they do not match any team based on their SSO groups.

notable_absence.finding: Prerequisite gate is generic and unlinked: 'To be signed in to the Ping admin console as an admin.' Same shape as CyberArk/Okta/OneLogin's informal wording.

cross_component_finding: Two real anomalies on this page, both worth a coordinator's attention: (1) a raw, unrendered template artifact leaks into the published content - the SAML attribute-mapping table is immediately followed by the literal text '{footnote-1}' with no corresponding footnote anywhere on the page, indicating a broken AsciiDoc footnote macro that failed to render into markdown - a genuine docs-issue candidate, not an ontology finding. (2) Ping's SAML attribute-mapping table includes a fifth attribute, `saml_subject` -> User ID, that no other provider's equivalent attribute-mapping step requires: CyberArk, Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta, and OneLogin all map exactly email/given_name/family_name/groups (four fields) and none map a subject/User ID attribute. This is either a real Ping-specific SAML requirement (PingOne needs an explicit subject NameID mapping other IdPs infer automatically) or a documentation inconsistency where other providers omit a step they also need - the six-provider template's 'clean parameterization' hypothesis breaks down exactly here. Also unique to Ping among the OIDC flows: an explicit 'Resources' tab step during app creation ('On the Application screen, click the Resources tab. Click Save.') with no stated purpose, and a final 'enable the application by clicking the toggle switch' step that Okta/OneLogin/Google fold into user assignment rather than a separate enablement toggle (CyberArk's SAML flow has an analogous separate enable step; Ping's OIDC flow duplicates it a second time for OIDC).
